title: Ala Singh and Patiala
hookLine: the Phulkian chiefs founded the states of Patiala, Nabha and Jind

lines: A WELL, A FEW HOUSES, A MARKET.
cards: A mud fort goes up on open ground in the Malwa country, south of the Sutlej. A well. A few houses around it.
A market that starts with a handful of stalls.
That's how some towns start, and Patiala, now a busy city in Indian Punjab, is remembered as starting something like that, around a fort built by a Sikh chief named Ala Singh.
His family line had a name of its own, and a story that goes back to a Guru.

teach.h: PHUL: THE BOY THE GURU BLESSED.
teach.b: The family were the Phulkians, named for an ancestor called Phul. Phul means flower. Tradition tells a story about him as a small boy.

He was brought, with his brother, before Guru Har Rai. The boys were hungry, and Phul patted his stomach. Tradition says the Guru took it as a sign and blessed him: his descendants would have enough, and would feed many.

The Phulkian families remember that blessing as the root of what came after. And what came after: Ala Singh, one of Phul's line, built up his holdings in these hard decades and founded the town and state of Patiala.
Other branches of the same family founded the states of Nabha and Jind. So in the middle of the decades of persecution, some Sikh families weren't only riding and hiding.
They were laying out streets, digging wells, building forts and markets. Then, honesty.

teach.h: A FOUNDER'S STORY, TENSIONS LEFT IN.
teach.b: Ala Singh's story isn't a simple hero's tale. He dealt with more than one power to keep his state alive, and tradition records that this put him at odds at times with other Sikh leaders.
This path tells it with that tension left in. Last, the small piece.
Every town you've lived in began somewhere: a crossing, a fort, a mill, a well. Someone chose that spot, and people kept coming.

how: The history of the Phulkian states of Patiala, Nabha and Jind, and the tradition of Guru Har Rai's blessing of Phul, is told in Sikh and Punjabi histories.

practice: Picture the place you live, then take away the newest buildings, the roads, the wires, until you're looking at whatever was there first: a river crossing, a fort, a farm, a station, a church or a temple or a well.
You may not know the real answer, and that's fine; just wonder who chose that spot, and who kept coming. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.
